analysis.one_liner: Orders the government to break up banks deemed 'too big to fail' and cut off their federal support.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on June 1, 2015 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Treasury Secretary to break up any financial institution large enough that its collapse would threaten the U.S. or global economy without a taxpayer rescue. Banks on that list would be barred from borrowing from the Federal Reserve, including in emergencies, and barred from using federally insured customer deposits to fund speculative trading in derivatives. Congress never took it up; it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, taxpayers would no longer be on the hook to rescue giant banks, and insured depositors' money would be walled off from risky derivatives trading. Small and regional banks, which never qualified for bailout backing, would have competed on a more level field with giants no longer implicitly guaranteed by the government.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Treasury Secretary to break up any institution whose failure would cause catastrophic effects on the U.S. or global economy without a taxpayer bailout, within one year of enactment. [S3]

Bars listed institutions from access to any Federal Reserve credit facility, discount window, or other program under the Federal Reserve Act, eliminating the emergency-lending safety net for the largest banks. [S3]

Prohibits institutions on the list from using federally insured deposits to fund speculative derivatives trading, hedging unrelated to core banking, or any activity that could cause losses to the Deposit Insurance Fund. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The largest U.S. banks and bank holding companies would bear the cost of being restructured into smaller firms, losing Federal Reserve backstops and implicit 'too big to fail' protection. Wall Street trading operations would lose access to insured deposit funding.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Treasury Secretary one year to break up complex, trillion-dollar institutions and consults the entity's own primary regulator, a compressed and potentially disruptive mandate that critics said could destabilize markets and slow lending if executed hastily. [S3]

Completely excluding the largest banks from all Federal Reserve programs, including emergency lending, removes a tool that can stop a financial panic from spreading to ordinary borrowers and depositors, a concern Dodd-Frank's approach of regulating rather than dismantling was designed to address. [S3]
The ban on speculative use of insured deposits overlaps substantially with the Volcker Rule already in law after Dodd-Frank, adding regulation for banks already covered by existing rules. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending the implicit federal guarantee that lets the biggest banks borrow more cheaply than everyone else and shifts crisis losses to taxpayers — would have been real and structural. The costs are execution risk: forcing breakups of enormous institutions on a one-year clock, and cutting them off from all Fed facilities, could have caused turbulence in credit markets that ordinary households feel. The design puts the burden of proof on the giants, but the schedule is aggressive.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, so the bill died in committee when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Brad Sherman on June 1, 2015, with Rep. Alan Grayson as an original cosponsor, and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services. [S1]
The committee took no further action; the full action history shows only introduction and referral. [S5]
The bill attracted just two cosponsors, both Democrats. [S4]
No version of the bill was ever considered on the House floor or in the Senate during the 114th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Wall Street banks, which kept their 'too big to fail' status, Federal Reserve access, and implicit government backing because the bill never advanced. The House Financial Services Committee's decision to hold no hearing meant the proposal never faced a recorded vote.

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Too Big To Fail, Too Big To Exist Act and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jeb Hensarling (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it dead in committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both cosponsors were Democrats and the Republican-led Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill, so support was entirely from one party.

industries.industry: Largest U.S. bank holding companies and systemically important banks
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to shrink, stripped their access to Federal Reserve lending, and cut off insured deposits from speculative trading — ending the implicit bailout guarantee that gives them a funding cost advantage over smaller banks. Their interest in the bill's defeat ran directly against taxpayers and depositors.

industries.industry: Wall Street derivatives and trading desks
industries.note: Banks on the list could no longer use federally insured customer deposits to fund speculative derivatives dealing, shrinking a major profit center built on subsidized funding.
Competitors without implicit government guarantees would face giants whose size advantage — cheaper borrowing premised on a taxpayer rescue — was eliminated or sharply reduced.
